lesson.title: A hypothesis and its revision in the same notes
lesson.text: When notes cover a scientific idea that was later revised, headings such as "Original hypothesis", "Problems with it" and "Revised view" divide the notes by stage. The passage uses similar vocabulary for all three stages (infection, exposure, microbes, hygiene). Before writing, confirm that your answer comes from the stage named in the heading above the gap.
lesson.example: Headings: "Original view: caused by (1) ______" and "Revised view: caused by (2) ______". The passage gives both causes in consecutive paragraphs; each answer must come from the matching stage.

questions.evidence: infections in early childhood, spread by contact with older siblings, might protect against allergies.
questions.explanation: "Brothers and sisters" (Paragraph A) is three words and exceeds the limit; "siblings" gives the same meaning in one word.

questions.evidence: it was widely reported as meaning that modern homes were simply too clean.
questions.explanation: This is the popular interpretation, which the notes label separately from the scientific claim.

questions.evidence: some viral infections actually increase the risk of asthma.
questions.explanation: This belongs to the "Problems" stage. "Allergies" is what the original hypothesis tried to explain.

questions.evidence: the Hutterites, who use industrial farming methods.
questions.explanation: "Methods" is already in the notes. "Industrial" alone is also acceptable.

questions.evidence: dust from Amish homes contained far more microbial material.
questions.explanation: "Far more" is already in the notes.

questions.evidence: exposure to the microorganisms with which humans evolved over millions of years.
questions.explanation: This is the revised view. "Infections in general" is what the revised view rejects.

questions.evidence: help train the immune system to tolerate harmless substances.
questions.explanation: The note needs a verb after "help the immune system".

questions.evidence: Handwashing and clean water prevent serious infections.
questions.explanation: "Handwashing and" is already in the notes.

lesson.title: Chains of cause and effect across paragraphs
lesson.text: Hard science passages explain a chain: a chemical is released → it rises → it is broken apart → it destroys something. Notes may present each link as a separate line, and a single link may be explained in one paragraph while its consequence is described in another. Follow the chain in order, and make sure the word you choose belongs to the link the note describes.
lesson.example: Passage: "Sunlight breaks the molecule apart, releasing chlorine, which destroys ozone." Note: "released by sunlight: (1) ______" Answer: chlorine (not "ozone", which is destroyed).

questions.evidence: This ozone layer absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation.
questions.explanation: "Ultraviolet radiation" is two words; adding "harmful" makes three, still within the limit.

questions.evidence: used in refrigerators, air conditioners and aerosol sprays.
questions.explanation: The other two items are already in the notes.

questions.evidence: ultraviolet radiation would break them apart, releasing chlorine atoms, each of which could destroy many thousands of ozone molecules.
questions.explanation: This is the last link of the chain before ozone is destroyed. "Ozone molecules" are what is destroyed, not what destroys.

questions.evidence: measuring ozone above their research station at Halley Bay ... using ground-based instruments.
questions.explanation: "British Antarctic Survey" is the organisation, not the location.

questions.evidence: ozone levels over Antarctica in spring had fallen by around a third since the 1960s.
questions.explanation: "Around" = "about". "Since the 1960s" is already in the notes.

questions.evidence: programmed to reject extremely low readings as probable errors.
questions.explanation: "Rejected as" matches directly.

questions.evidence: clouds form in the stratosphere, and chemical reactions on the surfaces of their ice particles convert chlorine.
questions.explanation: "Stratospheric" is already in the notes.

questions.evidence: the first United Nations treaty to be ratified by every member state.
questions.explanation: This is three words, within the limit.

questions.evidence: may return to its 1980 levels by around the 2060s.
questions.explanation: "2060s" alone is also acceptable. 1980 is the target level, not the date of recovery.

lesson.title: Very compressed notes
lesson.text: Some notes are compressed into almost pure symbols and abbreviations: "est. 1m pieces 1–10 cm: too small to (2) ______". Expand each note into a full sentence before searching ("An estimated one million pieces between one and ten centimetres are too small to ..."). The expanded sentence will be much easier to match to the passage, and it shows you the grammar the gap needs.
lesson.example: Note: "pop. ↑ 3× since 1950". Expanded: "The population has tripled since 1950."

questions.evidence: Space agencies track more than thirty thousand objects larger than about ten centimetres.
questions.explanation: "Over" = "more than". "A million" is the estimate for smaller pieces.

questions.evidence: around a million pieces between one and ten centimetres across, too small to track.
questions.explanation: Expanded, the note reads "An estimated one million pieces ... are too small to track". The gap needs a verb.

questions.evidence: its most vulnerable parts are protected by layered shields.
questions.explanation: "Layered" is already in the notes.

questions.evidence: producing still more fragments in a chain reaction.
questions.explanation: "Chain" is already in the notes.

questions.evidence: In 2007, China tested an anti-satellite missile by destroying one of its own old weather satellites.
questions.explanation: The Russian satellite was involved in the 2009 collision, not the 2007 test.

questions.evidence: collided accidentally over Siberia.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.evidence: removed within twenty-five years of the end of their missions.
questions.explanation: "Yrs" = "years", already in the notes. A hyphenated number counts as one word.

questions.evidence: companies launch large constellations of thousands of small satellites to provide internet services.
questions.explanation: "Internet satellite" is already in the notes.

questions.evidence: successfully tested a net and a harpoon.
questions.explanation: "Robotic arms" are another method being developed, not part of the 2018 test.

lesson.title: Final review — the complete Note Completion method
lesson.text: This final set combines all the main skills: matching abstract headings to the passage, expanding compressed notes, following a process in order, separating a claim from its criticism and its defence, and copying the minimum words within the limit. For each gap: (1) identify the heading's section; (2) expand the note into a sentence; (3) find the matching idea; (4) copy the exact words and check the limit and grammar.

questions.evidence: can be used only when paintings contain carbon, such as charcoal.
questions.explanation: "Such as" = "e.g.".

questions.evidence: mineral pigments such as red ochre ... which contain no carbon.
questions.explanation: "Red" is already in the notes. "Iron oxide" is what ochre is made of, not the pigment's name.

questions.evidence: water trickling over the walls deposits thin layers of calcium carbonate.
questions.explanation: "Stalactites" are formed by the mineral; they are not what covers the paintings.

questions.evidence: the uranium gradually decays into thorium at a known rate.
questions.explanation: The arrow means "decays into".

questions.evidence: its age gives a minimum age for the art beneath: the painting must be older.
questions.explanation: Expanded, the note reads "The age of the crust is the minimum age of the painting".

questions.evidence: If this was correct, the art must have been made by Neanderthals.
questions.explanation: "Modern humans" had not yet arrived in Europe, which is why the claim points to Neanderthals.

questions.evidence: if water dissolves and removes some of the uranium ... a process called leaching ... the crust will appear older than it really is.
questions.explanation: This is the critics' point, under the heading "Criticism".

questions.evidence: suggesting that they might be natural stains.
questions.explanation: "Natural" is already in the notes.

questions.evidence: taking several samples through each crust, from the surface inwards.
questions.explanation: This is the dating team's defence. "Inwards" is already in the notes.

lesson.title: Work row by row
lesson.text: In an easy table, each row usually comes from one paragraph. Find the paragraph that describes the item in the row heading, then look for the details asked for by each column. Finish one row before you move to the next, and the answers will follow the order of the passage.
lesson.example: Row "Parchment", column "Made from". Go to the paragraph about parchment and look for the material: animal skin.

questions.evidence: a tall reed that grew along the River Nile.
questions.explanation: "Along" = "beside".

questions.evidence: it decayed quickly in damp climates.
questions.explanation: This is the drawback column. "Dry" describes where papyrus survives, the opposite.

questions.evidence: Parchment was made from animal skin, usually that of sheep, goats or calves.
questions.explanation: "Sheep, goats or" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: it could be folded into pages.
questions.explanation: This is the advantage column. "High cost" is already given as the drawback.

questions.evidence: A wooden board was hollowed out and filled with a layer of beeswax.
questions.explanation: "Stylus" is the writing tool, not what filled the board.

questions.evidence: the writing could easily be erased or melted.
questions.explanation: "Erased or" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: plant fibres, such as tree bark, hemp and old rags.
questions.explanation: "Old" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: could be produced in large quantities.
questions.explanation: "Large" is already in the cell.

lesson.title: The column heading tells you the type of answer
lesson.text: Before searching, look at the column heading and the other cells in that column. A column headed "Typical span" needs a distance or number; a column headed "How the load is carried" needs a part of the structure. Predicting the type of word first stops you from choosing a detail that belongs in a different column.
lesson.example: Column: "Year opened". Other cells: 1890, 1932. Gap: (3) ______ Answer type: a year.

questions.evidence: a horizontal beam supported at each end.
questions.explanation: "Each" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: suitable only for short spans, usually less than about eighty metres.
questions.explanation: The column heading "Typical span" predicts a number. "Metres" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: They are cheap and quick to build, which makes them common on motorways.
questions.explanation: "Common on" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: it can be made from materials that are strong in compression, such as stone.
questions.explanation: "Steel wire" is the material for suspension cables, the next row.

questions.evidence: two main cables, which pass over tall towers.
questions.explanation: "Tall" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: can be affected by strong winds, which may cause the deck to move.
questions.explanation: The plural matches the passage.

questions.evidence: they run directly from one or more towers to the deck.
questions.explanation: "From towers to the" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: the number built has increased sharply since the 1970s.
questions.explanation: 2022 is the opening year of a suspension bridge, the previous row.

lesson.title: When the gap is the row heading
lesson.text: Sometimes the gap is in the first column: you are given the description and must supply the name of the item. Read the other cells in the row (where it is found, its special features), find the paragraph that matches them, and take the name from that paragraph.
lesson.example: Row: "(1) ______ | lives in Arctic | white fur". Paragraph: "The polar bear lives in the Arctic; its fur appears white." Answer: polar bear.

questions.evidence: The dromedary, or Arabian camel, has a single hump and is found mainly in North Africa, the Middle East and India.
questions.explanation: The other cells in the row (one hump, the regions) identify the paragraph, and the name comes from it.

questions.evidence: temperatures that can fall below minus thirty degrees Celsius.
questions.explanation: "Minus" and "degrees" are already in the cell.

questions.evidence: the wild Bactrian camel, survives in small numbers in the Gobi Desert.
questions.explanation: "Central Asia" is where the domesticated Bactrian camel lives, the row above.

questions.evidence: it is able to drink salty water that other mammals cannot.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.evidence: used by the Incas and earlier peoples mainly as a pack animal.
questions.explanation: "A" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: Llamas are sometimes used today to guard flocks of sheep.
questions.explanation: "Dogs and foxes" are what llamas chase away, not what they guard.

questions.evidence: does not contain the natural oil found in sheep's wool.
questions.explanation: "Lacks natural" = "does not contain the natural".

questions.evidence: It comes in more than twenty natural colours.
questions.explanation: "More than" and "natural colours" are already in the cell.

lesson.title: Words already in the cell
lesson.text: Table cells are short, so most of the phrase is often already printed and only one word is missing. With ONE WORD ONLY, read the cell carefully and ask which single word completes it. If the passage says "shale become slate" and the cell says "slate (from mudstone or ______)", you need only "shale".
lesson.example: Cell: "made from shells and (1) ______". Passage: "made from shells and skeletons". Answer: skeletons.

questions.evidence: Igneous rocks form when molten rock cools and becomes solid.
questions.explanation: "And becomes solid" is already in the cell. "Erupts" describes only volcanic rocks.

questions.evidence: pumice, contain so many gas bubbles that they can float on water.
questions.explanation: "Can" and "on water" are already in the cell.

questions.evidence: the layers are buried, compressed and cemented together.
questions.explanation: "Buried, compressed and" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: they are the only type in which fossils are commonly found.
questions.explanation: "Commonly found" = "common".

questions.evidence: changed by intense heat and pressure ... without melting.
questions.explanation: "Heat and" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: mudstone and shale become slate.
questions.explanation: "Mudstone or" is already in the cell. "Limestone" becomes marble, not slate.

questions.evidence: slate, which splits easily into thin sheets and has long been used for roofs.
questions.explanation: "Sculptors" relates to marble, not slate.

lesson.title: Dates and periods in a table
lesson.text: A column headed "Date" or "Origin" may need a year (1642), a decade (the 1850s) or a century (the fourteenth century). Look at the exact wording in the cell: "by the ______" and "from the ______" usually need a decade or century. When the passage gives two dates for one device (first desktop models and first pocket models), the other cells in the row tell you which one fits.
lesson.example: Row: "Pocket radio | early (1) ______". Passage: "Desktop radios appeared in the 1920s; pocket radios followed in the 1950s." Answer: 1950s.

questions.evidence: the suanpan, was in use by the fourteenth century at the latest.
questions.explanation: "By the" in the cell needs a period, here a century.

questions.evidence: it is still used in parts of Asia to teach children mental arithmetic.
questions.explanation: This is the strengths column.

questions.evidence: Pascal's machine used a series of interlocking gear wheels.
questions.explanation: "Interlocking" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: they were expensive and difficult to repair.
questions.explanation: This is the weaknesses column; "expensive" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: two rulers marked with logarithmic scales.
questions.explanation: "Scales" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: they gave results to only about three significant figures.
questions.explanation: "Three" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: The arithmometer, produced in France from the 1850s.
questions.explanation: "From the" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: in the early 1970s pocket calculators became available.
questions.explanation: The row is about pocket calculators. The early 1960s is when desktop electronic calculators appeared.

lesson.title: Comparison tables and similar rows
lesson.text: A comparison table asks for the same kind of information about several similar items: here, the habitat, food and social life of four apes. Because the items are similar, the passage uses similar words for each one (fruit, forest, groups). Check that the detail you choose belongs to the ape named in the row.
lesson.example: Row "Chimpanzee | main food: (1) ______". Both orangutans and chimpanzees eat fruit, but you must take the answer from the chimpanzee paragraph.

questions.evidence: Their diet consists mainly of fruit, supplemented by leaves, bark and insects.
questions.explanation: "Mainly" is already in the cell. Chimpanzees also eat mainly fruit, but this row is about orangutans.

questions.evidence: orangutans are largely solitary.
questions.explanation: "Largely" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: Their diet is mainly leaves, stems and shoots.
questions.explanation: "Leaves, stems and" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: usually led by a single mature male called a silverback.
questions.explanation: The gap needs a noun after "a".

questions.evidence: Chimpanzees live across a wide belt of Africa, in forests, woodland and savanna.
questions.explanation: "Forest, woodland and" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: they are known to hunt monkeys in cooperative groups.
questions.explanation: "Termites" are fished out with tools, which is not hunting.

questions.evidence: large communities of up to around a hundred and fifty individuals.
questions.explanation: A number fits the limit. "Around" = "about".

questions.evidence: females hold high status and form strong alliances.
questions.explanation: "Hold high" is already in the cell.

lesson.title: Cells that contain lists
lesson.text: At Medium level, one cell often contains a short list separated by semicolons: "olive oil; whale oil; from the 1860s, (3) ______". The passage gives the items of the list in different places, sometimes in different sentences. Read the items that are already printed, find them in the passage, and look for the missing item near them, checking any condition in the cell ("from the 1860s").
lesson.example: Cell: "wheat; barley; later (1) ______". Passage: "Early farmers grew wheat and barley; maize arrived much later." Answer: maize.

questions.evidence: In the nineteenth century, candles made from paraffin wax ... became common and cheap.
questions.explanation: "Later" in the cell points to the nineteenth-century material, the last item of the list.

questions.evidence: Candles made from beeswax burned cleanly and brightly but were so expensive.
questions.explanation: This is the problems column; "burned cleanly" is an advantage.

questions.evidence: From the 1860s, kerosene, refined from petroleum, replaced whale oil.
questions.explanation: The condition "from the 1860s" in the cell identifies it. "Petroleum" is what kerosene was refined from.

questions.evidence: a lamp with a hollow, circular wick and a glass chimney.
questions.explanation: "Glass" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: Gas was produced by heating coal.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.evidence: London's first gas-lit street appeared in 1807.
questions.explanation: 1780 is the date of Argand's lamp, in the row above.

questions.evidence: gas lamps produced heat and soot, consumed oxygen, and occasionally caused explosions.
questions.explanation: "Occasional" = "occasionally caused".

questions.evidence: a thin carbon filament that glowed when an electric current passed through it.
questions.explanation: "Carbon" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: releasing most of the energy they used as heat rather than light.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

lesson.title: Comparisons and quantities in cells
lesson.text: Some cells express a comparison ("uses less than (5) ______ the energy of distillation") or a quantity with its unit ("only a few (8) ______ per square metre daily"). Read the whole cell and decide exactly what is missing: the size of the difference, the unit, or the thing being compared. Then find the passage sentence that makes the same comparison.
lesson.example: Cell: "costs about (1) ______ of the old method". Passage: "It costs roughly a third as much as the old method." Answer: a third.

questions.evidence: Seawater is heated until it evaporates ... and the steam is then cooled to produce fresh water.
questions.explanation: "Then cooled" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: can treat very salty or dirty water.
questions.explanation: "Very salty or" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: they are often built next to power stations so that they can use waste heat.
questions.explanation: "Waste heat" is the reason for the location, not the location itself.

questions.evidence: seawater is forced at high pressure through a semi-permeable membrane.
questions.explanation: Both "membrane" and "semi-permeable membrane" (a hyphenated word counts as one) are within the limit.

questions.evidence: Reverse osmosis often uses less than half the energy of distillation.
questions.explanation: This is the comparison. "Ninety-seven per cent" and "one and a half litres" are different quantities.

questions.evidence: the membranes can become blocked by particles, algae and bacteria.
questions.explanation: "Can become" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: droplets condense on the cover and run down into a collecting channel.
questions.explanation: "Sloping" in the cell describes the sheet that forms the cover.

questions.evidence: typically a few litres per square metre per day.
questions.explanation: Only the unit is missing.

lesson.title: Many similar numbers
lesson.text: A passage comparing systems may contain a dozen numbers that look alike (365, 354, 365.25, 260). The table tells you which number you need by its row and column: the row names the system and the column names the measurement. Before you choose a number, say in words what it measures ("the length of the Islamic year").
lesson.example: Passage: "Planet A orbits in 88 days; Planet B in 225 days." Row: "Planet B | orbit (days): (1) ______". Answer: 225.

questions.evidence: it gradually drifted out of line with the seasons, by one full day every four years.
questions.explanation: "Years" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: The Egyptians, however, also tracked the rising of the star Sirius.
questions.explanation: "The star" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: The Islamic calendar is purely lunar.
questions.explanation: The other cells in the Basis column ("solar") show that an adjective is needed.

questions.evidence: giving a year of about 354 days.
questions.explanation: "Thirty-three" is the number of years before festivals return to the same season, not the length of the year.

questions.evidence: it was still about eleven minutes longer than the true solar year.
questions.explanation: "Ten days" is the accumulated error by the sixteenth century, not the yearly error.

questions.evidence: Britain did not change until 1752.
questions.explanation: 1582 is when the calendar was introduced, and 1918 is when Russia changed.

questions.evidence: a 365-day solar calendar and a 260-day ritual calendar.
questions.explanation: 365 is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: The two combined in a cycle of fifty-two years, known as the Calendar Round.
questions.explanation: A hyphenated number counts as one word.

lesson.title: When the rows are in a different order from the passage
lesson.text: Tables often arrange rows logically (by date, by size) rather than in the order the passage describes them. Here the rows run from the oldest battery to the newest, but the passage discusses the most widely used type first. Do not assume that row 1 comes from the first paragraph. Find each row by its name.
lesson.example: Table rows: "Bronze Age | Iron Age". Passage order: Iron Age (Paragraph B), then Bronze Age (Paragraph C). The first row's answers are in Paragraph C.

questions.evidence: the lead-acid battery, invented by the French physicist Gaston Planté in 1859.
questions.explanation: The first row comes from Paragraph C, not B. 1800 is the date of Volta's first battery, which was not a lead-acid battery.

questions.evidence: Lead-acid batteries are also among the most recycled products in the world.
questions.explanation: "Very widely" matches "among the most".

questions.evidence: the large bursts of current needed to start car engines.
questions.explanation: "Starting car" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: They are robust and perform well in cold conditions.
questions.explanation: "Robust" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: Cadmium is also highly toxic.
questions.explanation: This is the weaknesses column.

questions.evidence: It was commercialised in 1991.
questions.explanation: 2019 is the year of the Nobel Prize, not of commercial use.

questions.evidence: they depend on materials such as lithium and cobalt, whose mining raises environmental and social concerns.
questions.explanation: "Lithium and" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: sodium, which can be obtained cheaply from salt and is far more abundant than lithium.
questions.explanation: "Far more" is already in the cell.

lesson.title: Units in the column heading
lesson.text: When a column heading includes a unit, such as "Distance (km)", the cells in that column contain only numbers. Write the number without the unit. Other units in the same passage (litres, years, hours) belong to different columns or different facts.
lesson.example: Heading: "Height (m)". Passage: "The tower is 324 metres tall." Answer: 324.

questions.evidence: to a small area of mountain forest in central Mexico.
questions.explanation: "Central" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: travel up to about four thousand kilometres.
questions.explanation: The heading already gives the unit (km), so write only the number.

questions.evidence: an internal clock located in their antennae.
questions.explanation: "A clock in their" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: following the rains that produce fresh grass.
questions.explanation: "Fresh grass" is what the rains produce, not what the animals follow.

questions.evidence: warm, shallow lagoons on the coast of Mexico, where females give birth.
questions.explanation: "Mexican" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: The round trip can exceed sixteen thousand kilometres.
questions.explanation: "Exceed" = "over"; the unit is in the heading.

questions.evidence: swim thousands of kilometres to the Sargasso Sea in the western Atlantic Ocean.
questions.explanation: "Atlantic Ocean" is the wider area, not the destination named.

questions.evidence: no one has ever observed eels spawning there.
questions.explanation: The gap needs a past participle after "has never been".

lesson.title: The grammar of the cell
lesson.text: Table cells are not full sentences, but they still have grammar. "may (4) ______ in hot water" needs a verb; "good (3) ______" needs a noun; "(2) ______ easily" needs a verb that fits "easily". With ONE WORD ONLY, the passage word must fit exactly in its original form, so the grammar of the cell helps you choose between possible words.
lesson.example: Cell: "may (1) ______ in sunlight". Passage: "The colour can fade in strong sunlight." Answer: fade. A base verb fits after "may", and it is the exact passage form.

questions.evidence: grows as a soft, fluffy mass around the seeds of the cotton plant.
questions.explanation: The gap needs a plural noun after "the".

questions.evidence: cotton fabric creases easily.
questions.explanation: The verb form "creases" fits "fabric ______ easily".

questions.evidence: which traps air and makes wool an excellent insulator.
questions.explanation: The gap needs a noun after "excellent".

questions.evidence: wool can shrink badly if washed in hot water.
questions.explanation: The base verb fits after "can".

questions.evidence: Silk is produced by the larvae of the silk moth, which spin cocoons.
questions.explanation: "Silk moth" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: has a natural shine.
questions.explanation: "Natural" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: it does not absorb moisture well.
questions.explanation: Cotton also absorbs moisture, but as an advantage; this row is about nylon's drawback.

lesson.title: "How it works" columns
lesson.text: A column headed "How it works" or "Method" needs a part or a process, not a result. The passage usually explains a technique in two steps: what it consists of, and what that achieves. If the cell describes the achievement already ("... resist sideways forces"), the gap needs the component that produces it.
lesson.example: Cell: "rubber (1) ______ absorb vibration". Passage: "Rubber pads under the machine absorb vibration." Answer: pads.

questions.evidence: The building is separated from its foundations by flexible bearings.
questions.explanation: This is the component; "separate building from foundations" is the result already in the cell.

questions.evidence: works best for low and medium-rise buildings on firm ground.
questions.explanation: This is the limitation column.

questions.evidence: The Taipei 101 tower in Taiwan contains a steel sphere weighing more than six hundred tonnes.
questions.explanation: "Steel" is already in the cell. "Six hundred tonnes" is its weight, not what it is.

questions.evidence: diagonal steel braces, often arranged in an X-shape, strengthen the frame.
questions.explanation: "Diagonal steel" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: a building that is too stiff can attract larger forces.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.evidence: their flexible joints allow movement.
questions.explanation: "Flexible" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: Strengthening older buildings, known as retrofitting, is also important, but it is costly.
questions.explanation: The limitation column needs the problem, here expressed as an adjective.

lesson.title: Advantages that are expressed indirectly
lesson.text: Passages often express an advantage without using the word "advantage": "Because trains never encounter traffic, metros are fast and reliable." The table column "Advantage" collects these statements. Look for positive evaluations (fast, cheap, reliable, far less) and for reasons introduced by because or since.
lesson.example: Passage: "Since trams run on electricity, they produce no exhaust in the street." Column "Advantage": "no street (1) ______". Answer: exhaust.

questions.evidence: The first, in London, opened in 1863.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.evidence: Because trains never encounter traffic, metros are fast and reliable.
questions.explanation: The advantage is expressed through "because". "Fast and" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: their permanent tracks are thought to encourage investment along their routes.
questions.explanation: "May" in the cell reflects "are thought to".

questions.evidence: stations where passengers pay before boarding.
questions.explanation: "Pay before" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: capacity approaching that of a metro at a small fraction of the cost.
questions.explanation: "Small" and "of the cost" are already in the cell.

questions.evidence: it requires taking road space from cars.
questions.explanation: This is the disadvantage column.

questions.evidence: In Medellín, Colombia, a cable car system opened in 2004 connects poor hillside neighbourhoods to the metro.
questions.explanation: "Medellin" without the accent is also accepted. "Curitiba" and "Bogotá" are BRT examples.

questions.evidence: but their capacity is limited.
questions.explanation: "Limited" is already in the cell.

lesson.title: Hard Table Completion — claim, evidence and criticism columns
lesson.text: Hard tables often compare theories, with columns for the main claim, the supporting evidence and the criticism. Each paragraph of the passage contains all three, but the passage does not label them. Look for signals: "supporters argue", "draws support from", "points to" introduce evidence; "critics", "however", "its weakness" introduce criticism. Place each detail in the right column before you choose an answer.
lesson.example: Passage: "The theory is supported by fossil footprints, but critics note that the footprints are poorly dated." Column "Criticism": "footprints poorly (1) ______". Answer: dated.

questions.evidence: whereas their vocal calls appear to be largely fixed and tied to particular emotions.
questions.explanation: "Whereas" signals the contrast that the theory uses as evidence.

questions.evidence: Critics point out that it remains unclear why a fully developed gestural system would have been abandoned for speech.
questions.explanation: "Critics" signals the criticism column.

questions.evidence: to express emotion and attract partners.
questions.explanation: "Expressed emotion" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: infants respond to melody and rhythm in speech long before they understand words.
questions.explanation: "Draws support from" signals the evidence column.

questions.evidence: Its weakness is that it does not explain how meaning became attached to sounds.
questions.explanation: "Its weakness" signals the criticism column.

questions.evidence: replacing the grooming that monkeys and apes use to maintain relationships.
questions.explanation: "Gossip" is how talking works, not what it replaced.

questions.evidence: much everyday conversation still concerns social matters.
questions.explanation: "Points to" signals evidence.

questions.evidence: the theory explains why language was useful rather than how it began.
questions.explanation: The cell repeats the passage structure; "not how it began" is already printed.

questions.evidence: making complex stone tools activates brain areas that overlap with those involved in processing language.
questions.explanation: "Brain-imaging" in the passage is hyphenated, but the cell needs only the kind of activity: brain.

lesson.title: Years and technical terms spread across rows
lesson.text: In Hard passages about research, several dates and technical terms appear close together, and some belong to later additions to a model ("In 2000, Baddeley added a fourth component"). When a cell asks for a year, decide whether it means the original proposal or a later change. When it asks for a term, check which component or process the row and column describe.
lesson.example: Passage: "The theory was proposed in 1950 and revised in 1972." Cell: "Proposed (year): (1) ______". Answer: 1950.

questions.evidence: short-term memory, which can hold only around seven items.
questions.explanation: "Twenty to thirty" is the number of seconds, not items.

questions.evidence: unless they are repeated, a process known as rehearsal. Information that is rehearsed enough is transferred to long-term memory.
questions.explanation: The gap needs a noun after "through".

questions.evidence: studies of patients with brain damage.
questions.explanation: "Brain" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: Critics argued, however, that it was too simple.
questions.explanation: "Too" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: In 1974, Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch proposed the working memory model.
questions.explanation: 2000 is when the episodic buffer was added, a later change, not the original proposal.

questions.evidence: Baddeley added a fourth component, the episodic buffer.
questions.explanation: "Episodic" is already in the cell; "added later" signals the 2000 change.

questions.evidence: Evidence came from dual-task experiments.
questions.explanation: "-task experiments" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: deep processing, which involves thinking about meaning, produces stronger ones.
questions.explanation: "Capital letters" is an example of shallow processing.

questions.evidence: 'depth' is difficult to define and to measure.
questions.explanation: Either verb completes the cell correctly; only one word is allowed.

lesson.title: The same word in different rows
lesson.text: In Hard comparison passages, the same word may appear in the description of several items. Here "soil" appears both as a carbon store for forests and as something that rock dust may improve. The row and column together decide which occurrence you need. Before writing a repeated word, check that it comes from the paragraph about the item in your row.
lesson.example: Row: "Method B | benefit: better (1) ______". "Water" is mentioned for Method A and Method B; take the answer only from Method B's description.

questions.evidence: store carbon in their wood and in the soil.
questions.explanation: This is the storage column of the reforestation row. "Soil" appears again in Paragraph D, but there it is something that is improved, not a store.

questions.evidence: forests can be destroyed by fire, disease or logging.
questions.explanation: "Fire, disease or" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: pumped deep underground into rock formations, where it can remain for thousands of years.
questions.explanation: "Underground" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: the amount of carbon stored can be measured precisely.
questions.explanation: The gap needs an adverb after "measured".

questions.evidence: Its main drawbacks are cost and energy use.
questions.explanation: "High cost" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: carried to the ocean and stored as carbonate for very long periods.
questions.explanation: "Basalt" is the rock, not the form in which carbon is stored.

questions.evidence: the rock dust may also improve soil quality and crop yields.
questions.explanation: This is the benefits column of the weathering row, the second occurrence of "soil".

questions.evidence: Ocean fertilisation involves adding iron to areas of the ocean.
questions.explanation: "Phytoplankton" is what grows, not what is added.

questions.evidence: scientists raised concerns about possible harm to marine ecosystems.
questions.explanation: "Possible harm to" is already in the cell.

lesson.title: The same detail for more than one row
lesson.text: Sometimes a detail appears in the passage for two different items. Here both cholera and influenza were carried by troops, and two epidemics were caused by the same bacterium. A detail that belongs to one row may be the trap for another. For each gap, return to the paragraph about the item in that row and check that the answer is stated for that item.
lesson.example: Passage: "Both the dog and the fox hunt at night, but only the fox stores food." Row "Dog | habit: (1) ______". Answer: hunts at night; "stores food" belongs only to the fox.

questions.evidence: The Plague of Justinian struck the Byzantine Empire in 541.
questions.explanation: "The 2010s" is when the bacterium was identified, not when the plague began.

questions.evidence: DNA recovered from the teeth of victims buried in Germany.
questions.explanation: "Victims'" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: although the scale of its impact is disputed.
questions.explanation: "Scale of impact" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: The disease was spread mainly by fleas carried by rats.
questions.explanation: "Mainly" rules out "lice", which only some researchers believe played a major role.

questions.evidence: surviving labourers could demand higher wages.
questions.explanation: "Higher" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: Cholera is transmitted through water contaminated with human waste.
questions.explanation: Cholera was also carried "by troops", but the cell asks how it is transmitted, which is through water.

questions.evidence: a major force behind investment in sewers and clean water supplies.
questions.explanation: "And clean water supplies" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: The movement of troops at the end of the First World War helped it spread.
questions.explanation: This detail is also true of cholera, but here it is stated for influenza in Paragraph E, so it fits this row. "Spain" is only where the disease was first widely reported.

lesson.title: Challenges that come from other people
lesson.text: In a table of theories, the "Limitation or challenge" column may contain a finding by a different researcher (Leontief's test of the Heckscher–Ohlin theory), or a problem that the next theory was designed to solve (the weakness in Smith's theory that Ricardo addressed). The answer for one row may therefore appear in the paragraph about the next person. Read each theory's paragraph and the paragraph that follows it.
lesson.example: Passage: "Theory X could not explain Y. Theory Z was later proposed to solve this." Row "Theory X | weakness: could not explain (1) ______". Answer: Y.

questions.evidence: exporting as much as possible and importing as little as possible, accumulating gold and silver.
questions.explanation: "Gold and" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: if one country can produce a good more efficiently than another.
questions.explanation: The gap needs an adverb after "produces more".

questions.evidence: in which its opportunity cost is lowest.
questions.explanation: "Opportunity" is already in the cell. The limitation of Smith's theory, in the row above, is the problem Ricardo's theory solved.

questions.evidence: it assumes that workers and resources can move easily between industries.
questions.explanation: The gap needs an adverb after "move".

questions.evidence: export goods that make intensive use of the factors of production they have in abundance.
questions.explanation: "Scarce" describes the factors used by imports, the opposite.

questions.evidence: Leontief ... found that American exports were, surprisingly, more labour-intensive than its imports.
questions.explanation: The challenge comes from a different economist, Leontief, in the same paragraph. "Capital" is another factor, but it is not the finding.

questions.evidence: emphasised economies of scale: producing on a large scale lowers costs.
questions.explanation: "Economies of" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: while consumers benefit from greater variety.
questions.explanation: "Greater" is already in the cell.

lesson.title: Final review — the complete Table Completion method
lesson.text: This final set combines all the main skills: identifying each row's paragraph, placing details in the claim, evidence and weakness columns, choosing between several similar numbers and dates, and copying the minimum words. For each gap: (1) name the row and column; (2) predict the type of answer from the column and the neighbouring cells; (3) find the detail in the paragraph about that row; (4) check the word limit and the grammar of the cell.

questions.evidence: extinctions often followed soon after humans arrived in a region.
questions.explanation: The gap needs a verb after "humans".

questions.evidence: moas disappeared within about two centuries of human settlement around 1300.
questions.explanation: 1300 is the date of settlement, not the length of time.

questions.evidence: relatively few sites preserve clear evidence of humans killing extinct megafauna.
questions.explanation: "Critics note" signals the weakness column.

questions.evidence: open grasslands ... were replaced in many areas by forests.
questions.explanation: "Steppe" is what shrank, not what replaced the grasslands.

questions.evidence: some extinctions coincide with rapid climate changes.
questions.explanation: "Supporters point out" signals the evidence column.

questions.evidence: the megafauna had survived many earlier cycles of warming and cooling.
questions.explanation: "Many earlier" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: while human hunting delivered a final blow.
questions.explanation: "A" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: a small group survived on Wrangel Island in the Arctic Ocean.
questions.explanation: "Island" is already in the cell.

questions.evidence: a comet struck North America around 12,900 years ago.
questions.explanation: "Ten thousand years ago" (last mainland mammoths) and "four thousand years ago" (Wrangel Island) belong to other rows.

lesson.title: Follow the sequence words
lesson.text: In an easy flow-chart, the passage describes the process step by step, using sequence words such as begins, then, next and finally. Each box normally matches one or two sentences, in the same order. Find the sequence word that starts each stage, and look for the answer within that stage before moving on.
lesson.example: Passage: "Next, the ink must be removed." Box: "de-inking: ink ... removed". This box matches the stage introduced by "Next".

questions.evidence: it is separated into grades, such as newspaper, cardboard and office paper.
questions.explanation: "Such as" = "e.g.".

questions.evidence: it is placed in a large vat called a pulper.
questions.explanation: "Pulp" is the result, which is already in the box.

questions.evidence: Screens remove unwanted items such as staples, plastic and glue.
questions.explanation: The gap needs a plural noun before "remove".

questions.evidence: The ink particles stick to the air bubbles, rise to the surface and form a foam.
questions.explanation: "Air" is already in the box.

questions.evidence: If white paper is required, the pulp may also be bleached.
questions.explanation: "Required" = "needed".

questions.evidence: The cleaned pulp is then sprayed onto a moving mesh screen.
questions.explanation: "Moving" is already in the box.

questions.evidence: then over heated cylinders that dry it.
questions.explanation: "Rollers" squeeze out water; they are a different part of the stage.

lesson.title: ONE WORD in each box
lesson.text: With ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER, the gap is usually a key noun (a substance, a product) or a verb describing what happens (turned, added). Check the grammar of the box: after "slabs stacked and ______", you need a past participle to match "stacked".
lesson.example: Box: "dough kneaded and ______". Passage: "The dough is kneaded and then shaped into loaves." Answer: shaped.

questions.evidence: These bacteria convert the natural sugar in milk, lactose, into lactic acid.
questions.explanation: "Lactic" is already in the box.

questions.evidence: a substance called rennet is added. ... It causes the milk to set ... within about forty minutes.
questions.explanation: "Starter culture" was added in the previous stage.

questions.evidence: This is cut into small pieces, called curds.
questions.explanation: "Whey" is the liquid that is drained away, already in the box.

questions.evidence: large slabs, which are cut, stacked on top of each other and turned repeatedly.
questions.explanation: The past participle matches "cut, stacked and".

questions.evidence: The slabs are then cut into small pieces, a process called milling, and salt is mixed in.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.evidence: The salted curds are packed into moulds and pressed, often overnight.
questions.explanation: "Often overnight" is already in the box.

questions.evidence: mature or 'vintage' cheddar may be kept for more than two years.
questions.explanation: "Three months" is the time for mild cheddar.

lesson.title: Flow-charts with a list of options
lesson.text: When you choose answers from a list, the options are usually paraphrases rather than exact passage words, and there are more options than gaps. First decide the type of word each box needs (a place, a food, a colour, an action), then find the stage in the passage, and finally choose the option with the same meaning. Cross out each option as you use it.
lesson.example: Box: "young birds leave the (1) ______". Passage: "the chicks fly from the nest". Options: A tree B nest C ground. Answer: B.

questions.evidence: an adult female digs a shallow nest, called a redd, in the gravel of a fast-flowing stream.
questions.explanation: J (sand) is the same type of word but is not mentioned.

questions.evidence: alevins, which stay hidden in the gravel, feeding on a yolk sac attached to their bodies.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.evidence: the young fish emerge from the gravel and begin to feed on insects.
questions.explanation: C (shrimp) is food at sea, a later stage.

questions.evidence: Their bodies become silver.
questions.explanation: "Become" = "turn".

questions.evidence: they use the Earth's magnetic field to navigate across the ocean.
questions.explanation: This is the stage at sea.

questions.evidence: and then their sense of smell to identify their home river.
questions.explanation: The magnetic field is for the ocean crossing; smell is for the home river.

questions.evidence: Swimming upstream, adults leap waterfalls ... and stop feeding altogether.
questions.explanation: H (swimming) is the trap: they keep swimming upstream.

lesson.title: Times and temperatures in a process
lesson.text: Process passages often give several times and temperatures ("within twenty-four hours", "twenty to forty minutes", "below twenty-seven degrees"). The box tells you which one you need: a limit on time before processing, the length of a stage, or a maximum temperature. Check the words around the number in the passage, and do not copy the unit if it is already in the box.
lesson.example: Box: "baked at (1) ______ degrees". Passage: "The loaves are baked at 220 degrees for 30 minutes." Answer: 220.

questions.evidence: machines that shake the trees so that the fruit falls onto nets spread on the ground.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.evidence: Ideally they are processed within twenty-four hours.
questions.explanation: "Within" is already in the box. "Twenty to forty minutes" is the length of malaxation, a later stage.

questions.evidence: the fruit is washed in water.
questions.explanation: "In water" is already in the box.

questions.evidence: The whole olives, including their stones, are then crushed into a paste.
questions.explanation: "Including their" is already in the box.

questions.evidence: usually below twenty-seven degrees Celsius.
questions.explanation: "Degrees Celsius" is already in the box.

questions.evidence: Today most mills use a centrifuge, a machine that spins the paste.
questions.explanation: "Mats" belong to the traditional method.

questions.evidence: it is stored in stainless steel tanks away from light and air.
questions.explanation: "Stainless steel" is already in the box.
